title: Liverpool cannot afford any mistakes at Anfield against Galatasaray after wilting in Istanbul
content:
The giant banner unfurled behind the goal before kick-off read: “You are alone in Sami Yen Hell!’

It was a twist on Liverpool’s iconic ‘You’ll never walk alone’ anthem and a warning about the kind of challenge that Arne Slot’s side faced in Istanbul.

What followed was an incessant attack on the senses as the Premier League champions wilted in the Rams Park cauldron.

The damage done by Mario Lemina’s early header should be repaired in next Wednesday’s Champions League last-16 second leg at Anfield. This is no time to panic. Galatasaray are a lesser force on their travels — illustrated by the manner in which they threw away a 5-2 lead from the home leg in their play-off with Juventus in the previous round before eventually getting the job done with two extra-time goals in Turin, having played against 10 men for over an hour.

The Turkish champions were also beaten away in three of their four league-phase matches, by Eintracht Frankfurt, Monaco and Manchester City. And with the vociferous Galatasaray supporters banned by UEFA, European football’s governing body, from attending the decider on Merseyside, the odds are still stacked in Liverpool’s favour as they attempt to set up a quarter-final against either Chelsea or the holders Paris Saint-Germain, who knocked them out of this competition at this stage last season.

However, if Slot’s side are going to march on and be serious contenders for Champions League glory come May, they simply can’t afford another error-strewn night like this. A better team than Galatasaray would have made them pay a greater price for their inadequacies at both ends.

Ibrahima Konate’s performance was arguably the most concerning.

The France centre-back’s resurgence since the turn of the year has been crucial given Slot’s limited defensive options. Before Tuesday night, Konate had looked much more composed and commanding. But this was a throwback to earlier in the season when he looked so rash and nervy, and a succession of calamitous mistakes led to his head coach describing him as being “a bit too much on the crime scene”.

After inexplicably missing a Wilfried Singo cross, Konate was relieved to see Victor Osimhen fire over the bar before the break. He got even luckier in the second half when he made a mess of a back pass to goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili and then failed to clear again before Osimhen converted from close range.

Konate, who is on course to be out of contract at the end of the season, was lying on the turf distraught before realising that an offside flag had spared his blushes. It was a generous decision given that Baris Alper Yilmaz, the Galatasaray player involved, didn’t actually touch the ball in the build-up.

The defender’s miserable night was compounded when Dominik Szoboszlai’s corner bobbled into the net off him for an apparent equaliser that was quickly ruled out due to handball. Slot was adamant that incident should have resulted in a penalty being awarded by Spanish referee Jesus Gil Manzano.

“If you look at how much they pulled on Virgil (van Dijk)’s shirt before the ball hit Ibou’s (Konate) arm then it’s safe to say we were not the only one impressed by the atmosphere here,” Slot said.

“In the Premier League, there is much more (shirt-pulling) allowed than in the Champions League. That’s why I was so surprised it wasn’t a penalty. Even if we just looked at a Galatasaray player, the referee gave a free kick for Galatasaray.”

Konate completed just 22 of his 32 passes in the game, with his 68.8 per cent success rate lower than any other Liverpool outfield player who started the game. Given what’s at stake for Liverpool in the coming weeks, Slot needs him to quickly bounce back from this performance.

If Konate’s mind was scrambled by the din around him, then he wasn’t the only one. How else do you explain the sight of Florian Wirtz failing to hit the target inside two minutes with the net gaping after the visitors’ high press had resulted in Lemina giving the ball away just outside his own penalty area?

This was Wirtz’s first start for nearly a month due to a back problem, but rather than give Liverpool an injection of quality and creativity he was off the pace and horribly wasteful. The Germany international squandered another decent chance when he scuffed a shot straight at goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir after being teed up by Alexis Mac Allister.

By then Liverpool had fallen behind in painfully avoidable fashion from a corner. Neither Mac Allister nor Joe Gomez got off the ground to compete for a header with Osimhen and for some reason Milos Kerkez and Hugo Ekitike were standing together by the post when an unmarked Lemina nodded home.

“You have to give credit for the way, when they get a chance, they play as if it is the last chance of their lives,” Slot said. “That is definitely something we can learn from them, because we sometimes get our chances and it comes across as if we think we’ll get 10 more. It’s already a difficult place to go if you’re 0-0, but going one goal down made it even harder for us.”

Mamardashvili was one of the few to emerge with any real credit as he pulled off a couple of great saves. The manner in which the Georgian deputised for the injured Alisson was all the more impressive given that he’d played only once since November.

However, there was a distinct lack of control from Liverpool in midfield and not enough of a sustained threat going forward.

Mohamed Salah, who was making a club record 81st Champions League appearance, was fortunate to get past the hour mark before being replaced by Jeremie Frimpong. Ekitike was a willing runner throughout but couldn’t capitalise when faced with just Cakir to beat. Finishing that chance would have put a different complexion on the night.

Liverpool may have won both the Champions League final and the UEFA Super Cup in Istanbul, but they still haven’t beaten Turkish opposition in this city in six attempts (five defeats, one draw).

Last September, they recovered after a bruising 1-0 defeat here by Galatasaray and swiftly got their European mission back on track. Now they need to do likewise in only seven days.

“What I do know is now it’s half-time,” Slot added. “We’ve lost here twice and the good thing is the next game is not played here. It is played at Anfield and our fans can create a similar atmosphere. I don’t think it’s possible that so many things can go against us as happened in these two games. Things will be more normal in a home game for us and I also think we can improve our performance.”

If Liverpool deliver in that second leg, when it will be their crowd providing the soundtrack, then this noisy night will soon fade into obscurity. But if they fall short, there will be no hiding place.
